extracted.intended_audience: readers of literary criticism; students and practitioners of creative writing and literary biography
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic/biographical discussion of Frances Burney and Samuel Crisp that embeds evaluative principles about authorship, criticism, dramatic writing, and how literary merit is formed and judged. Useful as guidance for assessing fiction, drama, critics, and authorial practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who is fit to judge literature
rubrics_metrics.description: A connoisseur — one whose business is to judge and enjoy, with wide reading, taste, and sense — is more likely to appreciate works justly than either the unlearned multitude or a great original genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The crowd is dazzled by what stuns them; great original geniuses often lack balanced taste outside their own speciality and thus judge wrongly. Prefer judgments from informed, impartial connoisseurs rather than from popularity or from other specialised geniuses. Example: Gerard Douw and Michael Angelo would judge differently; an impartial connoisseur may see more justly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand and confine yourself to your talents
rubrics_metrics.description: One should understand the limits of one's powers and not attempt to attain distinctions that are unattainable given one's natural talents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambition to excel in a form unsuited to one's abilities leads to humiliation and wasted effort (Samuel Crisp's attempt to be a great dramatist). The prudent course is to recognize one's strengths and cultivate those rather than chasing inappropriate honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic quality: plot, characters, and diction
rubrics_metrics.description: A play (or dramatic work) is to be judged on its plot, characterisation, and diction; deficiencies in these aspects justify critical rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics in the Monthly Review attacked Crisp's Virginia on these grounds — plot, characters, and diction — suggesting these are primary criteria for dramatic success. Avoid feeble plot construction, unnatural characters, and awkward or inflated language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness over forced sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages intended to be sublime or pathetic must accord with nature; forced attempts at grandeur appear as tame extravagance and are counterproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers who 'set themselves to be sublime and pathetic in spite of nature' produce unnatural bursts that fail. Aim for emotions and sublimity that arise organically from characters and situations rather than rhetorical inflation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acquire varied, first-hand social observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Close, sustained observation of people across classes provides rich materials for fiction; the 'great book of human nature' is learned in life as much or more than from books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frances Burney’s exposure to a wide and varied company (from nobility to artists and tradespeople) gave her a store of materials for fiction few obtain. Writers should observe behavior, manners, and social interaction in diverse settings to build authentic scenes and types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and retain marked peculiarities of character
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctive, marked peculiarities in people catch and stay in the imagination, and are valuable raw material for fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even without an eye for fine shades, noting striking oddities or singular traits allows a writer to create memorable characters. Fanny’s habit of withdrawing to observe produced a catalog of peculiarities that later populated her fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material richness can outweigh formal literary knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: A writer’s small formal acquaintance with canonical books does not preclude producing major fiction if they possess energetic observation and invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burney wrote Evelina despite limited reading of major Continental authors and little novel-reading; direct experience and imagination compensated for lack of classical literary learning. Do not treat lack of broad bookish training as fatal if one has strong observational material and imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentorship and critical correspondence shape development
rubrics_metrics.description: Sustained mentorship and correspondence with a judicious critic/scholar (e.g., Samuel Crisp) can significantly form a young writer’s taste and skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crisp supplied counsel and became a formative influence on Burney; letters and critique help refine grouping, humour, and characterisation. Seek informed readers and mentors to critique work and guide maturation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication strategy and negotiating terms matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing how to publish (anonymously or not) and securing favourable terms requires guidance; lack of counsel can cost an author materially and strategically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burney accepted twenty pounds for Evelina and later regretted greater possible earnings due to lack of parental advice. Authors should obtain knowledgeable advice on publishers, contracts, anonymity, and the financial/ reputational stakes before signing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Success judged by comparison with established masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical esteem is often articulated by comparing a new work to the best earlier works (e.g., Evelina compared to Smollett).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative placement (how a new novel stands relative to canonical works) is a common evaluative move. Use such comparisons cautiously: they can illuminate quality but also reflect critical partialities or fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vanity and cultivate modesty in reception of praise
rubrics_metrics.description: A modest, grateful disposition toward praise preserves character; an author should record compliments carefully and keep perspective, writing for close sympathisers rather than public acclaim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burney enjoyed honours but retained modesty, recording praise for the eyes of a few trusted friends. Allow fame to be tempered by attachment to family, friends, and the original purposes of writing; avoid letting triumph corrupt the author's temperament or priorities.
